title: Steal the Principle, Not the Playbook
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership micro-essay argues that the near-universal instinct to copy successful leaders' methods directly — importing the triangle offense, the rank-and-yank system, the Good to Great habits — is a seductive trap that produces consistent failure. Solutions are context-specific and travel poorly because they depend on unique combinations of people, culture, and competitive moment that cannot be replicated by outsiders. The article contrasts two modes of learning from others: photocopy (what did they do?) versus reverse-engineer (why did it work there?). Atul Gawande's application of aviation checklist logic to surgery is the article's strongest example: Gawande did not import the aviation checklist, he extracted the underlying principle — that systematic verification reduces error — and then rebuilt a new tool appropriate to a different context. This translation move, the article argues, is where real leadership learning begins.
points: Solutions are context-specific and rarely travel well. They work because of a unique combination of people, culture, timing, and competitive environment — all of which belong to the originating organization and cannot be transferred wholesale to a different one.

Atul Gawande's surgical checklist is the article's central proof of concept: the aviation checklist was not imported into the operating room but reverse-engineered to extract the principle (systematic verification reduces error) and then rebuilt for a different context — with transformative results.

Leaders who study successful organizations do the most useful thing when they reverse-engineer rather than replicate: not 'What did they do?' but 'Why did it work there?' — and then translate that understanding to their own situation.

Phil Jackson's triangle offense illustrates the problem vividly: it worked because Michael Jordan and Scottie Pippen had basketball intelligence to improvise within the structure. Without that specific talent, the same system does not underperform — it collapses.

The distinction between mimicry (comfort, low effort) and translation (harder, more generative) is the practical dividing line between leaders who learn from studying others and leaders who merely experiment with borrowed tools.
quotes: When Phil Jackson won eleven NBA championships using the triangle offense, thousands of basketball coaches rushed to install it and failed.
Solutions, even grand ones, rarely travel well. They are context-specific and produce great outcomes because of the unique mix of ingredients present at that moment.

The triangle offense worked well for Jackson because he had Michael Jordan and Scottie Pippen, players of rare basketball intelligence who could improvise within the structure and share decisions on the fly to keep defenders off-balance. Give the same system to a roster without that instinct, and it doesn't underperform. It collapses.

When Atul Gawande studied aviation checklists and applied the idea to surgery, he did not import them into the operating room. He asked what principle made them work and then built a new tool for a new context — the surgical checklist. The result was one of the most consequential patient safety interventions in modern medicine.

Leaders who learn the most from studying others treat every success story as a puzzle to reverse engineer, not a photocopy to reproduce. They don't ask, 'What did they do?' Instead, they ask, 'Why did it work there?'
Stealing someone else's solution underestimates the unique circumstances that made it work. Borrowing the principle underneath it is where the real learning begins. That's the move worth making.
